one_liner: Rust parser-combinator library beating nom on JSON throughput, with error recovery and zero-copy output.
what_it_does: Chumsky is a Rust library for building recursive-descent parsers (PEGs, plus context-sensitive extensions) out of composable combinators like `just`, `choice`, and `recursive`, aimed at compilers, DSLs, binary protocols, and config formats. It is not a drop-in replacement for nom: you write a chumsky `Parser` expression tree instead of nom's function-signature-based parsers. Outputs can be zero-copy, holding references/slices into the original input rather than allocating, and the crate is generic over input, token, output, span, and error types.
how_it_is_fast: Parsers are built as a typed combinator tree that chumsky's internal optimizer (built on GATs) specializes at compile time, avoiding much of the dynamic dispatch overhead of naive combinator libraries. A 'check-only' mode validates input without constructing an output/AST at all, which is the fastest configuration in its own benchmark. Zero-copy string/byte-slice handling avoids per-token allocation, and the optional `stacker` feature (on by default) spills recursion state to the heap only when the native stack is close to exhausted, rather than paying a cost up front.
when_to_use: Writing a compiler, interpreter, or DSL parser where you want structured error recovery and multiple diagnostics per parse instead of failing on the first error
Parsing UTF-8 text or byte slices where zero-copy output (slices into the input) matters for throughput or memory
Validation-only workloads where you just need to know if input is well-formed (chumsky's check-only mode is the fastest path in its own JSON benchmark)
no_std/embedded targets that need a parser combinator library without the standard library
Grammars needing context-sensitivity (semantic indentation, raw strings) beyond plain context-free/PEG combinators
when_not_to_use: You need nom's streaming/incremental parsing model for partial network buffers; chumsky's API is not drop-in compatible with nom and expects the input available as a slice
You want the fastest full-AST parse in this exact benchmark family: winnow (178.91 us) beats chumsky's full-parse mode (210.43 us) on the same JSON workload
You need a fully stable, 1.0-guaranteed API today; the crate is at 0.13.0 and an open tracking issue (#543, 'Tracking: Stable 1.0') shows the API surface is still settling

You plan to share a single parser value across threads via `recursive()`: chumsky's source (src/lib.rs) imports `alloc::rc::Rc` and `core::cell::{Cell, RefCell}` for its recursive-parser machinery, and thread-safety is not documented, so Send/Sync should not be assumed without checking
You're on the latest Windows MSVC toolchain: an open issue (#815) reports a linker error from just `use chumsky;`, unresolved as of this session

integration.dependencies: always: hashbrown, unicode-ident, unicode-segmentation; optional (feature-gated): stacker (default-on), regex-automata, lexical, either, serde, bytes, railroad
integration.platforms: any — no_std-compatible (`#![cfg_attr(not(...), no_std)]`), no architecture-specific requirements found; Windows+MSVC has an open unresolved linker-error report (issue #815)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; internal `recursive()` support is built on `Rc`/`RefCell` (seen in src/lib.rs imports), so recursive parsers are likely not Send/Sync without extra wrapping
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false — different combinator API from nom; a nom parser must be rewritten, not ported, to use chumsky

gotchas: The headline check-only number (140.77 us) validates input without building any output tree — don't compare it directly to other libraries' full-parse numbers, including chumsky's own 210.43 us full-parse figure
recursive() parsers appear to rely on Rc<RefCell<_>> internally (inferred from src/lib.rs imports, not stated in the docs), a likely source of !Send/!Sync surprises
Open issue #798: parsers wrapped in `.ignored()` currently skip `map_with()`, which the maintainers call out as unexpected behavior
Open issue #159: error-recovery logic can affect how otherwise-valid input is parsed, i.e. enabling recovery is not purely additive
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Of the catalogued siblings, only winnow is a close substitute (also a Rust parser library beating nom on this exact JSON benchmark). Pick chumsky over winnow when you want combinator ergonomics, built-in error recovery, and rich diagnostics for a hand-rolled language/DSL grammar; pick winnow when raw full-parse throughput matters most, since it beats chumsky's full-parse mode (178.91 us vs 210.43 us) in chumsky's own table. The other siblings (flap, PAPAGENO, re2c, Pika Parser) target OCaml/C parser-generator or lexer-generator use cases, not Rust combinator parsing, so they aren't direct alternatives.
verified_claims_summary: In chumsky's own first-party criterion JSON-parsing benchmark, run on a single core of an AMD Ryzen 7 3700x, chumsky's check-only mode took 140.77 us (797 MB/s) and full parse took 210.43 us (533 MB/s), versus 526.52 us (213 MB/s) for nom (7.1/8 both used as dev-dependencies) — roughly 3.7x and 2.5x the throughput of nom on that one workload. rustc version and optimization flags are not stated in the benchmark writeup.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-16) — the GitHub repo is now an archived mirror after the project's move to Codeberg (codeberg.org/zesterer/chumsky), where development continues. MIT-licensed and distributed as an ordinary crate, but still pre-1.0 (v0.13.0), so treat the combinator API as subject to change.
